# How Google renders pages

Google renders nearly all pages with headless Chromium to index what users see, said it would miss most of today's web without it, and, extending Day 1's point that Gemini uses Google's crawling, said pages are rendered the same way for Gemini training (said at the event, not in Google's docs). Rendering is a detached, expensive system that fetches JavaScript, CSS and API calls, but not images or videos, through the crawler; Google's documentation queues every page that returns 200 unless it carries noindex, and content missing from the final DOM cannot be indexed. The renderer does not scroll or click and lacks permission-based browser APIs and WebGL; Google said it renders in a viewport about 10,000 pixels tall instead, a figure its documentation does not give (it speaks of a 'viewport expansion' that can miss infinite content). The documentation sets no upper limit on the render-queue wait (a community speaker said seconds to a couple of minutes), and Google said content can be missing because it has not appeared in time; a community speaker added that slow APIs can leave unresolved placeholders in the snapshot. Author's view: Erin Sparling's remark that content indexable without JavaScript 'can pass through without rendering' does not mean such pages skip rendering; it means content in the raw HTML does not wait for the slower rendering pass. Day 3 put rendering in time: Google renders a page either right after crawling or later through a queue, so content added by JavaScript is typically seen by indexing within a few hours and at worst within weeks, and Google said its logs show everything in the queue rendered within weeks (said at the event). Google's own speaker also said he would not claim that Google renders every URL on the internet (not in Google's docs). Author's view: Google's JavaScript guide says every page returning 200 is queued for rendering, and queued is not rendered, so critical content belongs in the server HTML. Day 1's second recording added that Google renders JavaScript-heavy pages from their HTML, CSS and JavaScript as a browser would, with the latest Chromium. A second recording of Day 2 confirmed Natalia Venditto's point that a server-rendered app reframed into the host page is fully indexable (said at the event), and John Mueller said Google drops a page with a noindex in its HTML without processing its JavaScript, while Google's guide says it may skip rendering.

## What to do

- Put everything indexing depends on (title, meta description, canonical, robots meta tag, main text and links) in the server HTML, and let JavaScript add enhancements only.
- Never block in robots.txt the JavaScript, CSS or API endpoints the renderer needs.
- Load lazy content when it enters the viewport, never on scroll or click, and treat the 10,000-pixel viewport as a margin, not a target.
- Wrap permission-based browser APIs and WebGL effects in feature detection with a fallback, so the main content renders without them.
- Do not judge Googlebot's rendering from client-side analytics, which the renderer may skip.

(Gary Illyes, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Used by the glossary term *Render queue*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google renders pages in two ways: immediately after crawling, or later through a queue-based process that runs elsewhere.
  <br><sub>`D3-C626` · Day 3, How long does it take to..? (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Extends [D2-C170](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Content that JavaScript adds to a page is typically seen by Google's indexing system within a few hours, and at worst within weeks.
  <br><sub>`D3-C627` · Day 3, How long does it take to..? (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Extends [D2-C172](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-10`, `DEV-REN-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said Google keeps saying it renders every URL on the internet and that he would say this is not true, though it is what he was told; he went on to say that Google's logs show the rendering queue cleared within weeks.
  > "we keep saying that we render every single URL on the internet. I would say that that's not true"
  <br><sub>`D3-C628` · Day 3, How long does it take to..? (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C256](../sessions/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-REN-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** According to Google's logs, everything in the rendering queue gets rendered within weeks.
  <br><sub>`D3-C629` · Day 3, How long does it take to..? (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Render queue*</sub>

## What Google's documentation says

- **[Docs]** Google's Inside Googlebot post warns that bloated inline base64 images, large blocks of inline CSS or JavaScript, or megabytes of menus can push a page's text or structured data past Googlebot's 2MB cutoff, and advises moving heavy CSS and JavaScript to external files and placing meta tags, the title, the canonical and essential structured data high in the HTML.
  <br><sub>`D1-C137` · Search Central blog (31 March 2026) · annotates Day 1, How crawling works · is the documentation · [Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/03/crawler-blog-post) · Used by `DEV-PRF-04`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says that when Google encounters a noindex rule it may skip rendering and JavaScript execution, so using JavaScript to change or remove a noindex robots meta tag may not work as expected.
  > "it may skip rendering and JavaScript execution"
  <br><sub>`D2-C854` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing · is the documentation · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Used by `DEV-REN-05`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's JavaScript SEO guide says Googlebot sends every page with a 200 HTTP status code to the rendering queue, whether or not it contains JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header tells Google not to index it, and Google uses the rendered HTML to index the page.
  <br><sub>`D2-C131` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · is the documentation · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Extended by [D3-C676](../sessions/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) · Used by `DEV-REN-01`, the glossary term *Rendering*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google says Googlebot and its Web Rendering Service identify resources that do not contribute to essential page content, such as reporting and error requests, and may not fetch them, so client-side analytics may not give a full or accurate picture of their activity.
  <br><sub>`D2-C164` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · is the documentation · [Fix Search-related JavaScript problems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/fix-search-javascript) · Used by `DEV-MON-04`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says Googlebot extracts links twice, from the HTML response before rendering and again from the rendered HTML, so links injected with JavaScript can be found if they use crawlable `<a href>` markup.
  <br><sub>`D2-C169` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · is the documentation · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Extends [D1-C040](../sessions/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-01`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says a page may wait in the render queue for a few seconds but that it can take longer, and it gives no upper limit.
  > "The page may stay on this queue for a few seconds, but it can take longer than that."
  <br><sub>`D2-C172` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · is the documentation · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Extended by [D3-C627](../sessions/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) · Used by `DEV-PRF-02`, `DEV-REN-01`, the glossary term *Render queue*</sub>

- **[Docs]** In Google's March 2023 SEO office hours, John Mueller said Google handles infinite scroll with viewport expansion, rendering a page like a very long phone, which is not very efficient and can miss content, so pagination links are strongly recommended.
  > "this is done through a technique called "viewport expansion", where we render a page like a very long phone."
  <br><sub>`D2-C200` · Google Search Central (SEO office hours transcript, March 2023) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · is the documentation · [March 2023 Google SEO office hours](https://developers.google.com/search/help/office-hours/2023/march)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google says its Web Rendering Service fetches the resources a page references through Googlebot, including JavaScript, CSS and XHR requests to APIs, but not images or videos.
  <br><sub>`D2-C206` · Search Central blog (3 December 2024), Search Central blog (31 March 2026) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · is the documentation · [Crawling December: The how and why of Googlebot crawling](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/12/crawling-december-resources), [Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/03/crawler-blog-post) · Used by `DEV-REN-04`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's documentation says Google supports web components and flattens shadow DOM and light DOM content when it renders a page, and that content not visible in the rendered HTML cannot be indexed.
  <br><sub>`D2-C235` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · is the documentation · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics), [Fix Search-related JavaScript problems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/fix-search-javascript) · Used by `DEV-REN-10`, the glossary term *Shadow DOM*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's JavaScript SEO basics says every page with a 200 status code is queued for rendering, whether or not it uses JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header says not to index it; for non-200 pages such as 404 error pages, rendering might be skipped.
  <br><sub>`D2-C257` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript · is the documentation · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Used by `DEV-REN-05`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's March 2023 SEO office hours say Google sees infinite-scroll content through viewport expansion, rendering a page like a very long phone, which is not particularly efficient and can miss infinite content.
  > "a technique called "viewport expansion", where we render a page like a very long phone"
  <br><sub>`D2-C273` · Google Search Central (SEO office hours transcript, March 2023) · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript · is the documentation · [March 2023 Google SEO office hours](https://developers.google.com/search/help/office-hours/2023/march) · Used by `DEV-URL-07`, the glossary term *Viewport expansion*</sub>

- **[Docs]** For effects that need WebGL, which Googlebot does not support, Google's guide to fixing JavaScript problems suggests skipping the effect or prerendering it with server-side rendering so that the content is accessible to Googlebot.
  <br><sub>`D2-C278` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript · is the documentation · [Fix Search-related JavaScript problems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/fix-search-javascript) · Used by `DEV-REN-08`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's guide to fixing Search-related JavaScript problems says its Web Rendering Service keeps no state across page loads: local storage, session storage and HTTP cookies are cleared.
  <br><sub>`D2-C828` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript · is the documentation · [Fix Search-related JavaScript problems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/fix-search-javascript) · Used by `DEV-REN-06`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's guide to fixing Search-related JavaScript problems says the Web Rendering Service may ignore caching headers and so use outdated JavaScript or CSS, and recommends content fingerprinting, which puts a hash of the content in the file name, as in main.2bb85551.js.
  <br><sub>`D2-C829` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript · is the documentation · [Fix Search-related JavaScript problems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/fix-search-javascript) · Used by `DEV-REN-06`</sub>

## Analysis

- **[Analysis]** The stage remark that content indexable without JavaScript can pass through without rendering does not mean such pages skip rendering, because Google's guide queues every 200 page for rendering; read it as: content already in the raw HTML does not depend on the slower rendering pass.
  <br><sub>`D2-C132` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Put everything indexing depends on (title, meta description, canonical, robots meta tag, main text and links) in the raw HTML so it is available without rendering, let JavaScript add enhancements only, and check the rendered HTML in URL Inspection for the rest.
  <br><sub>`D2-C133` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · Used by `DEV-REN-01`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Because Google flattens shadow DOM when it renders, content that Web Fragments places in a shadow root can in principle be indexed with the host page, but only if it appears in the rendered HTML; check that in URL Inspection rather than relying on a library's promise of indexability.
  <br><sub>`D2-C250` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Used by `DEV-REN-10`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Wrap permission-based features (location, payments, camera) and WebGL effects in feature detection with a fallback, so the main content renders when the API is missing or the permission is declined; never make indexable content wait for a permission prompt.
  <br><sub>`D2-C282` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript · Used by `DEV-REN-08`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Put critical content, links and meta tags in the server HTML: content that needs JavaScript reaches indexing only after rendering, usually within hours but sometimes weeks, and even Google's own speaker doubted that every URL gets rendered.
  <br><sub>`D3-C630` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, How long does it take to..?</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The stage doubt that every URL gets rendered sits beside Google's JavaScript guide, which says every page with a 200 status is queued for rendering unless a robots rule blocks indexing: queued is not the same as rendered, so do not rely on rendering for critical content.
  <br><sub>`D3-C676` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, How long does it take to..? · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Extends [D2-C131](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-REN-01`</sub>

## Built on these claims

The items of the developer and content kits that rest on this topic's claims.

- Requirement `DEV-IDX-11`: Use the Google-Extended robots.txt token to control Gemini training and grounding
- Requirement `DEV-MON-04`: Monitor Crawl stats and server logs for verified Googlebot traffic
- Requirement `DEV-MON-10`: Plan releases and fixes around Google's processing times, and judge results only after them
- Requirement `DEV-PRF-02`: Make JavaScript-generated content render quickly
- Requirement `DEV-PRF-04`: Keep each HTML response well under 2 MB and put the main content and JSON-LD early
- Requirement `DEV-REN-01`: Server-render the main content and everything indexing depends on (SSR, static generation or hybrid)
- Requirement `DEV-REN-02`: Have all indexable content in the DOM after load, without clicks, typing or scrolling
- Requirement `DEV-REN-03`: Lazy-load with native lazy loading or an IntersectionObserver, never with scroll events
- Requirement `DEV-REN-04`: Do not block JavaScript, CSS or API endpoints that pages need for rendering in robots.txt
- Requirement `DEV-REN-05`: Do not add, change or remove robots meta tags with JavaScript
- Requirement `DEV-REN-06`: Make rendering robust: no slow API dependencies and no unresolved placeholders
- Requirement `DEV-REN-08`: Feature-detect permission-based APIs and WebGL, and render the content without them
- Requirement `DEV-REN-10`: Keep indexable content out of iframes, and check web components in the rendered HTML
- Requirement `DEV-URL-01`: Make every navigational link an `<a>` element whose href holds a real URL
- Requirement `DEV-URL-07`: Back infinite scroll and load-more buttons with paginated URLs
- Glossary term *Lazy loading*
- Glossary term *Render queue*
- Glossary term *Rendering*
- Glossary term *Shadow DOM*
- Glossary term *Viewport expansion*
